accuracy.evidence: The approach follows Watson and Mason (2005) on learner-generated examples (make one, then one that looks different) and is honest about the evidence: Rawson and Dunlosky (2016) and Zamary, Rawson and Dunlosky (2016) found students often judge their own wrong examples as right, so every example in the lab is tested against its rule. Content facts checked: noun as a person, place or thing (England KS1 grammar glossary); even numbers as pairs with none left over (NC Y2 odd and even); a square as 4 equal sides and 4 right angles in any orientation (NC Y2 shapes in different orientations). The lab's square test is exact on grid vectors (equal squared lengths, zero dot products), so the turned square (sides root 5) passes and the 2-by-4 rectangle and any rhombus fail. Parameterised items checked at corners: 2n for n 4 to 9, 4n for n 2 to 9, (n-n%2)/2 for n 7, 11, 15 gives 3, 5, 7, and 2n for n 2 to 6 (m7 widened after the validator asked for 4+ distinct combinations).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: repeating the taught example as proof of understanding (prediction 1, m1), cosmetic changes such as 'the dog' or 'Dog!' counted as new (refused in the sort), an odd number accepted as an own example (prediction 2; 7, 9 and 13 leave a red counter over), the prototype-orientation slip that a turned square is a diamond (prediction 3, challenge, p5), rectangles and rhombuses taken for squares (each refused with its own reason), copying the given example as a 'fix' (refused in the fix scene), and checking by looks, length or size (scene 5 and challenge).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagownex is about generating, not sorting given cases: the learner picks their own numbers and sees counters paired in a tester, taps dots to build their own squares with an exact side-and-corner check that refuses a same-size, same-way-up copy, mends three broken examples without copying, and chooses the reason that applies the rule. It differs from 1007 flagnonex (sorting given triangles and near misses), 981 worked examples and 741 odd and even numbers; the 6-token shingle check against every flag lab is at most 4%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each point by trying it: dropping 9 or 7 in the tester shows a red counter and '1 left over: not even'; dropping 6 is refused as Miss Lee's own; building a 1-space upright square is refused as a copy while a turned square shows four right-angle marks and passes; a 4-by-2 rectangle is refused with 'the corners are square, but 2 sides are longer'; and a crossed tap order is caught with 'tap the 4 corners in order, going round'. The kid text only confirms what the tester and grid already showed.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options the lab then disproves: 'Leo says dog back. Does that show he understands?' (Yes, he got it right, is tempting because the answer is correct; the sort shows it is a copy); 'Mia's own even number is 9. Will 9 counters make pairs?' (the tester shows one left over); 'A square turned on a corner, still a square?' (No, it is a diamond, is the common prototype answer; the grid shows equal sides and square corners).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Clicked through all seven challenge questions at 390 px. Each wrong answer names its slip, for example 'run' gets 'That is the example you were given. A copy is not an example of your own.', 'table' gets 'Table is a thing, so it is a noun. Find a doing word', 'No, it is a diamond now' gets 'Turning a shape does not change its sides or corners', 'bee and bin' gets 'start the same, but they do not end with the same sound', and 'See if it is long or big' gets its own size message (re-mapped after the click-through, where it had borrowed the big-number message).

readability.evidence: Kid text Flesch-Kincaid grade 0.8 (limit 5.0 for family lessons); adult text 9.2 (limit 10.0). Sentences are short and concrete (counters, squares, castle, grandma, spoon). Canvas labels are short; feedback is one or two sentences naming what to look at.

no_filler.evidence: No filler phrases (gate clean). Each kid paragraph does one job: why repeating is not understanding, making new examples, checking with counters, and making examples look different. Adult paragraphs give the evidence (including its limits), the common mistakes, and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px phone screenshots in light and dark for all five scenes before and after Show me: six answer cards in a 2 x 3 grid over two labelled boxes; the tester with fourteen counters in two rows and seven number tiles in a 4 + 3 grid; a 6 x 5 dot grid about 56 px apart with two finished squares and right-angle marks, Miss Lee's small square beside the idea text (text narrowed after the first screenshot showed overlap); and three full-width fix and reason tiles. Real mouse drags and dot taps at 390 px worked for every scene.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: 'Copy: dog' and 'My own: dog' pairs, 'Test 8' style buttons for the tester, four square buttons (bigger square, turned square, long rectangle, copy of Miss Lee's) plus 'Clear my dots', and one button per fix and per reason with full aria-labels. The canvas aria-label carries the scene description and every piece of feedback; challenge feedback is a role=status live region; counters use red plus the words '1 left over' and squares get right-angle marks, so state is not shown by colour alone; the browser gate runs axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) in both themes.
